There's an old joke that every time Apple announces a new iPhone Pro, it says it's "the best iPhone we've ever made," as if that's somehow surprising.

Specifically, we expect to see another step toward the "all-glass" vision next year, ending a decade of incremental changes…

The evolution of the iPhone Pro line

If you line up the iPhone 12 Pro through the 16 Pro, I think most people would struggle to tell them apart at a glance, except for the switch from a notch to a Dynamic Island in 2022. The iPhone 17 Pro is only barely recognizable, mainly thanks to its elongated camera module and Cosmic Orange.

Sure, every generation gets new features, but to be fair: unless a particular feature is especially useful to you, you really need to skip at least two or three generations to make it worth upgrading for a noticeably better experience.

None of this is a criticism of Apple. The fact is that smartphones are mature technology now, at least in terms of conventional design. You don't see huge differences between adjacent generations because there's just very little left to improve year over year.

Apple is now starting to experiment with different designs, beginning with the iPhone Air, of course, plus the iPhone Duo—and we expect another major design leap next year, with the 20th anniversary model.

It's still a little unclear how Apple will position next year's design. Earlier rumors suggested it would be a standalone model, not part of the iPhone 19 Pro lineup, but other reports say it will be next year's Pro model. There's also the question of whether Apple will use sequential numbering, or skip a number to mark the milestone, so it might end up being called the iPhone 20 Pro.

Personally, I expect it to be the new iPhone Pro design, whether Apple calls it the 19 or 20. If so, the iPhone 18 Pro would be the last version of this six- or seven-year look.

I'll be skipping two generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I'll list what each year's model offers me separately. I'll skip improvements that don't matter to me personally or are completely useless, like going from a 6-core GPU to a 7-core GPU and GenLock.

Carried over from the iPhone 17 Pro

  • Center Stage front-facing camera for photos and video calls
  • Ultra-stable video
  • Dual-camera simultaneous recording
  • Telephoto lens upgraded from 5x to 8x
  • Telephoto sensor upgraded from 12MP to 48MP
  • ProRes RAW video
  • Longer battery life
  • Faster charging speeds

What's new on the iPhone 18 Pro

  • Larger maximum aperture on the main camera
  • Variable aperture on the main camera
  • Pro-level camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)
  • Third-generation Photographic Styles
  • Intelligent focus tracking
  • Cinematic effects added to standard video
  • Tap-to-zoom and rotate on the front-facing camera
  • Smaller Dynamic Island that can display three Live Activities at once
  • (Even) longer battery life
  • (Even) faster charging speeds

My personal… highlights

For me personally, at this stage I'm mainly watching for five features.

Variable aperture lens

While the most eye-catching feature is the variable aperture lens, I've mentioned before that expectations shouldn't be set too high for it. The maximum aperture is only slightly wider, and the sensor is still fairly small, so I don't expect to see a big difference in shallow depth-of-field effects.

However, a larger maximum aperture does let in more light, roughly equivalent to two-thirds of a stop. How much of a real-world difference that makes remains to be seen, but in theory it should mean shorter exposure times in Night mode. Since I use this feature a lot—often handheld—I'm looking forward to trying it out.

Pro-level camera controls

Being able to control shutter speed will definitely come in handy for things like tracking shots. Full white balance control will be helpful too. I also expect the histogram will be very useful when manually adjusting exposure.

I'm generally not a big fan of filters, whether shooting or editing later on the iPhone—I prefer traditional adjustments. So I rarely use the existing Photographic Styles, and I don't expect to use this latest version much more either. But I have to say, its film presets really intrigue me, so I'll definitely give them a try.

One of the biggest weaknesses of autofocus when shooting video is that when the subject is briefly blocked by another object, the camera may shift focus to that obstruction. Intelligent focus tracking claims to address exactly this problem, so I'll definitely be testing it thoroughly.

Cinematic effects added to standard video

The most-liked comment came from atonaldenim

I'm really looking forward to hearing your thoughts after using the 18 Pro for a while. I should probably upgrade myself—I'm still using a 12 Mini. (Rest in peace, Mini.)

The telephoto lens will be a surprise; it might make me accept that the phone is much heavier and bigger than the Mini. Right now I'm debating whether to pay the full $1,200 for a new 18 Pro, or get a used 16 Pro for around $700 or less, which is roughly where used prices are now.

(The 17 Pro and 18 Pro are still priced very close together, so I didn't consider the 17 Pro—I'd rather pay a little more and go with the 18 Pro.)

So if you feel the 18 Pro offers significant improvements over the 16 Pro in the areas you mentioned, I'd love to hear your thoughts. Thanks!

I said less than two months ago that Apple seemed to have given up on Cinematic video mode. I mentioned at the time that it was a shame, because if Cinematic video was done well, it would be a killer feature for anyone wanting to use their iPhone as a more serious video camera. So far, it sort of works, but it's always missing something; it's always just shy of getting there.

But it turns out I was wrong: one of the new features on the iPhone 18 is the ability to apply Cinematic video effects to standard-mode video.

Not having to decide in advance whether to use the mode is certainly convenient, but what interests me most is that Apple seems to be reinvesting in this feature. That means they've put in the work, so you can expect it to keep improving, much like Portrait mode did in its early days for photos. I'm looking forward to testing it.

These are the features I think will have the biggest impact on me personally. What about you? If you've already upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, which features drove that decision? Feel free to share in the comments.
